newsitem.title: MEXICO: Battle seen tough in emerging market derivatives.
newsitem.headline: Battle seen tough in emerging market derivatives.

text.p: Emerging markets that lag in developing derivative products will find competitors in other countries ready to offer products based on their underlying securities, stock market officials said Wednesday.

"If one country cannot determine whether its equity market is developed enough or its size is large enough to introduce a derivatives market, its global competitors will," Yu-Kyung Kim, director of securities research at the Korea Stock Exchange, said at a conference of the International Federation of Stock Exchanges.
"Competition among financial markets is no longer bounded by national boundaries," he said.
In general the market for those derivatives and the underlying equities is large.

William Barclay, vice-president of strategic planning with the Chicago Board Options Exchange, said that from 1973 to 1996, stock options and index options were traded in 23 countries, index options in 28 countries, and stock futures in five countries.
Several participants who came from countries with emerging markets said their local stock exchanges were planning to introduce more derivative products within the next year or so.
They could draw a lesson from what happened to Germany in the second half of the 1980s, said Albrecht Burger, executive vice-president of the Deutsche Boerse.

Institutions in London rushed in to sell derivatives based on Deutsche mark products, and the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange still dominates trade in Bund and three-month interest rate futures, he said.

"Our experience at DTB (the German options and futures exchange) shows that when the local marketplace does not provide the products which the market needs, someone else will provide them," Burger said.
Mexico lost opportunities during the crisis that followed the 1994 peso crash by not having a well-developed derivatives market, according to an exchange official.

Bernardo Gonzalez-Arechiga, executive vice-president of the Bolsa Mexicana de Valores, said volatility tripled for the stock index and increased by 10 times in the foreign exchange market after the peso crash.
"Mexico lost the potential benefits of a high volatility period to launch the new derivatives market," he said.
He added that regulations would be published within the next few weeks to complete the legal framework for a new listed derivative market.

While competition is tough when it comes to introducing derivatives, certain instruments such as stock market indexes often fail to sustain a liquid market outside their home market, participants at the conference said.
The Mexican IPC index futures traded in Chicago have not been successful, Gonzalez-Arechiga said.
The CBOE's Barclay noted there have been no cases when an equity index derivatives market has been "captured" outside its home country.
"It is hard. Equity products seem to be much more rooted in home markets" than products such as currencies, he said.

Gilberto Mifano, chief executive officer at the Bolsa de Valores de Sao Paulo, said, "The most successful derivatives product in Brazil were based on cash or spot markets that were relatively big in terms of number of participants and trading volume."
